newsitem.title: KENYA: World loses track of Zaire's million refugees.
newsitem.headline: World loses track of Zaire's million refugees.

text.p: In the age of satellites, it is still possible to lose more than one million people -- the wretched refugees of eastern Zaire.

Two weeks after a rebel offensive in the area, aid agencies who for more than two years provided a lifeline for the Rwandan and Burundian Hutu exiles, at a cost of $1 million a day, admit they have no precise idea of the refugees' whereabouts.

"These people are running for their lives," said U.N. refugee agency spokesman Peter Kessler, referring to more than half-a-million people whose camps were in the first area to fall two weeks ago to Tutsi rebels along Zaire's eastern border.
"It is a mystery as to exactly where they are."
The fate of 700,000 more who were in camps around the city of Goma further north -- more than half of them in Mugunga, the world's biggest refugee camp -- was little clearer.

"How can we lose so many people in this day and age?" said Jordi Riach of Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors without Borders) which is trying to get its medical staff back to east Zaire from four different directions but so far without success.

If there are few black holes left on earth, eastern Zaire is one of them. Just away from the lakes that form the border with Rwanda and Burundi, the mountains rise, the jungle thickens, the villages get fewer and farther apart and paved roads fade away.
"This is one of the world's inaccessible regions," said Kessler. "There are virtually no roads."
African diplomats are to meet in Ethiopia to further a plan for a protection force -- on Monday next week. Britain and France will discuss the same -- but not until Friday.
As the days pass by, aid agencies fear that intervention will come too late for many of the homeless people.
Hunger, thirst, disease and exposure to rain and cold loom. "You can die of hypothermia even on the Equator," Kessler said.
Agencies said most refugees will be running out of the last supplies of flour, cornmeal and sugar they were given.
Experts say the fittest could live two weeks with next to no water or food. The fate of children, the old and ill is dimmer.
Hundreds of Zairean aid staff stayed when the foreigners fled. A few managed to carry their radios and heavy car-battery power supply with them, but contacts have petered out.
A worker for CARE International provided the last news at the weekend of some 200,000 people who fled one of the northernmost camps, Katale, last week.
Sticking with 20,000 of the weakest, he said they had sat down on a mountainside, exhausted and thirsty, to die.
There are no reports from local authorities or journalists, UNHCR lost contact with its helpers in Mugunga five days ago.

The UNHCR believes most of Mugunga's 400,000 people have fled some 15 km (10 miles) west, where the tarred road runs out. But other agencies believe Mugunga is still full, though few seem quite sure where their information first came from.
Fleeing refugees have reported many deaths at the camp.
Urgently requested satellite photographs to assess the flight, which the United States provided in Bosnia and elsewhere to help humanitarian relief, have failed to materialise.
"We have had no word back from the Americans. It's been two weeks now," said Chris Cushing of CARE International.
Only one Argentinian doctor is known to have stayed on in rebel-held territory, performing amputations at his home by flashlight with a Swiss army knife.

Several thousand people -- the bulk of them brand new Zairean refugees -- have trickled eastwards into neighbouring Uganda, Tanzania. Some Burundians have gone home, back to the Hutu-Tutsi civil war they fled which is still raging there.
The U.N. urges Rwanda's million exiles to go home, but they fear revenge for the 1994 genocide of up to a million people, mainly Tutsis.
Hutu militiamen blamed for the genocide had the run of the camps and use refugee families as a buffer to protect them.
They are still believed to be herding them west or north, stopping anyone who would like to from going home to Rwanda.
Humanitarian workers worry that dysentery, diarrhoea, typhus and cholera -- which claimed 50,000 lives in two months when the refugees fled to Zaire in 1994 -- will soon be back.
"A catastrophe comparable to the events of 1994 is looming,"said the International Federation of the Red Cross.
